sk: ब्रह्मा देवानां प्रथमः सम्बभूव विश्वस्य कर्ता भुवनस्य गोप्ता स ब्रह्मविद्यां सर्वविद्याप्रतिष्ठामथर्वाय ज्येष्ठपुत्राय प्राह ||
ro: brahmā · devānāṁ · prathamaḥ · sambabhūva · viśvasya · kartā · bhuvanasya · goptā · saḥ · brahma-vidyāṁ · sarva-vidyā-pratiṣṭhām · atharvāya · jyeṣṭha-putrāya · prāha ||
hi: ब्रह्मा — जो देवताओं में प्रथम (सबसे पहले) प्रकट हुए, विश्व के कर्ता (रचयिता) और भुवन (लोक) के गोप्ता (रक्षक) हैं — उन्होंने ब्रह्मविद्या को — जो सब विद्याओं की प्रतिष्ठा (आधार/मूल) है — अपने ज्येष्ठ पुत्र अथर्वा को कहा (सिखाया)।
en: Brahmā — who arose first among the gods, the creator of the universe, the protector of the world — taught brahma-vidyā (the knowledge of Brahman), the foundation of all knowledge (sarva-vidyā-pratiṣṭhā), to his eldest son Atharvā.

ws.e: Brahmā — the four-faced creator god; the first being to arise in the cosmic cycle; distinct from Brahman (the Absolute)
arose / came into being — sam + √bhū (to become); Brahmā was the first to manifest in creation
the knowledge of Brahman — the supreme knowledge; the subject-matter of this Upanishad

ws.h: सब विद्याओं की प्रतिष्ठा / आधार / मूल
ws.e: the foundation of all knowledge — sarva (all) + vidyā (knowledge) + pratiṣṭhā (foundation); brahma-vidyā is the base upon which all other knowledge rests
to Atharvā — Brahmā's eldest son; the legendary originator of the Atharvaveda; the first recipient of brahma-vidyā
to the eldest son — jyeṣṭha (eldest) + putra (son); the knowledge passes to the firstborn, establishing a lineage

gr: The knowledge-lineage (vidyā-paramparā): the Muṇḍaka opens by establishing the chain of transmission — Brahmā → Atharvā. This is not merely a historical claim but a statement of authority: brahma-vidyā does not originate from human speculation but from the Creator himself. sarva-vidyā-pratiṣṭhā — 'the foundation of all knowledge': a bold claim. All other knowledge (science, grammar, ritual, etc.) rests upon brahma-vidyā, because Brahman is the ground of all reality. Know the ground, and you understand everything that stands upon it. brahmā devānāṁ prathamaḥ — 'Brahmā, the first among the gods': Brahmā (the created deity, masculine) is distinguished from Brahman (the Absolute, neuter). Brahmā is the first being to arise within creation; Brahman is the source from which creation arises. Even Brahmā needs to learn brahma-vidyā — he is not Brahman but the first knower of Brahman.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_1.1.1 — The Muṇḍaka Upanishad belongs to the Atharvaveda (specifically the Śaunaka school). The opening lineage (Brahmā → Atharvā) connects the Upanishad directly to the Atharvaveda's mythical founder. The term 'sarva-vidyā-pratiṣṭhā' is unique to the Muṇḍaka and will be elaborated in mantras 4-5 where parā and aparā vidyā are distinguished. The Muṇḍaka is one of the three Upanishads (along with Īśā and Śvetāśvatara) that form the 'Prasthāna-traya' sources — Shankara's commentary on the Muṇḍaka is one of his most important. The name 'Muṇḍaka' means 'shaving/razor' — traditionally interpreted as the Upanishad that 'shaves off' ignorance.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — ब्रह्मा स्वयं ब्रह्म नहीं — ब्रह्म के प्रथम ज्ञाता (first knower) हैं। 'सर्वविद्याप्रतिष्ठा' — ब्रह्मविद्या इसलिए सब विद्याओं का आधार है क्योंकि ब्रह्म सब का आधार है। कारण (cause) को जानने से कार्य (effect) स्वतः ज्ञात हो जाता है।
advaita.en: Shankara says Brahmā is not Brahman himself but the first knower of Brahman. 'Sarva-vidyā-pratiṣṭhā' — brahma-vidyā is the foundation of all knowledge because Brahman is the foundation of all reality. Know the cause, and all effects are automatically known.
advaita.ins: Even the Creator had to learn. Brahmā — the first being — received brahma-vidyā. He didn't invent it; he received it. That tells you something: this knowledge is not created by any mind. It is the structure of reality itself.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — ब्रह्मा भगवान् (नारायण) की प्रथम सृष्टि और प्रथम शिष्य दोनों हैं। भगवान् ने सृष्टि के आरम्भ में ब्रह्मा के हृदय में ब्रह्मविद्या का बीज स्थापित किया — वहाँ से यह ज्ञान-परम्परा प्रारम्भ हुई।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says Brahmā is both the Lord's (Nārāyaṇa's) first creation and first disciple. At the beginning of creation, the Lord planted the seed of brahma-vidyā in Brahmā's heart — from there the knowledge-lineage began.
vishisht.ins: The first student in the universe was Brahmā. And his teacher was God Himself. The knowledge you're about to receive has been passed down in an unbroken chain from the Creator to his firstborn to his firstborn's student — all the way to you.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — ब्रह्मा = सार्वभौम चेतना (universal consciousness) का प्रथम व्यक्तीकरण (individualisation)। 'सर्वविद्याप्रतिष्ठा' — ब्रह्मविद्या सब ज्ञान की नींव है क्योंकि चेतना (consciousness) सब अस्तित्व (existence) की नींव है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says Brahmā = the first individualisation of universal consciousness. 'Sarva-vidyā-pratiṣṭhā' — brahma-vidyā is the foundation of all knowledge because consciousness is the foundation of all existence.
aurobindo.ins: All knowledge — science, art, philosophy — rests on one knowledge: the knowledge of consciousness itself. Know consciousness, and you hold the master key. Every other key opens one door; this key opens all of them.

dp.a: The Muṇḍaka opens by establishing a lineage of transmission (vidyā-paramparā) for brahma-vidyā. This is not a historical footnote but a foundational claim about how sacred knowledge works: The chain: Brahmā → Atharvā → (mantras 1-2 will complete the chain to Aṅgiras). This lineage connects the Upanishad to the beginning of creation — the knowledge is as old as the universe itself. Why lineage matters: in the Vedic tradition, knowledge is not 'discovered' by individual genius but received (śruti = 'that which is heard') from a teacher who received it from their teacher, in an unbroken chain going back to the divine source. This makes the knowledge: (1) Authoritative — it doesn't come from human opinion but from the structure of reality itself. (2) Tested — it has been transmitted, practised, and verified across countless generations. (3) Living — it is not a dead text but a living transmission between teacher and student. Why Brahmā? Brahmā is the 'first knower' — the first conscious being in the cosmic cycle. If even Brahmā needed to learn brahma-vidyā (rather than possessing it innately), this implies that brahma-vidyā is not a property of any individual but a discovery of the universal structure — available to anyone who seeks it through the proper means. Parallel lineages: the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (2.6, 4.6, 6.5) contains extensive vaṁśa (lineage) lists. The Chāndogya (3.11.4) traces knowledge from Brahmā through Prajāpati. The Bhagavad Gītā (4.1-2) traces yoga-knowledge from Vivasvān (the Sun) through Manu and Ikṣvāku.

dp.q: 🔍 Why is brahma-vidyā called 'the foundation of all knowledge'?
dp.a: The compound sarva-vidyā-pratiṣṭhā ('the foundation of all knowledge') makes a sweeping claim: brahma-vidyā is not one knowledge among many but the base upon which all other knowledge rests. The logic: Brahman is the cause (kāraṇa) of everything that exists. All objects, all processes, all beings originate from Brahman. Therefore: (1) Knowledge of any object is ultimately knowledge of Brahman-as-that-object. (2) Physics, chemistry, biology, psychology — all study aspects of Brahman's manifestation. (3) Knowing Brahman directly is like knowing clay directly: once you know clay, you know all clay-pots, clay-cups, and clay-plates (Chāndogya 6.1.4-6). The Chāndogya analogy: Uddālaka tells Śvetaketu: 'By knowing one lump of clay, all clay-products are known — the modification is a name-word only, the reality is clay.' Similarly, by knowing Brahman, all modifications (the universe) are known — the modifications are nāma-rūpa (name and form) only, the reality is Brahman. Practical implication: this doesn't mean brahma-vidyā replaces physics or medicine. It means that brahma-vidyā provides the framework within which all other knowledge finds its meaning. A physicist studies the laws of nature; brahma-vidyā reveals whose nature those laws describe.

sk: अथर्वणे यां प्रवदेत ब्रह्मा ऽथर्वा तां पुरोवाचाङ्गिरे ब्रह्मविद्याम् स भारद्वाजाय सत्यवाहाय प्राह भारद्वाजो ऽङ्गिरसे परावराम् ||
ro: atharvaṇe · yāṁ · pravadet · brahmā · atharvā · tāṁ · purā · uvāca · aṅgire · brahma-vidyām · saḥ · bhāradvājāya · satyavāhāya · prāha · bhāradvājaḥ · aṅgirase · parāvarām ||
hi: अथर्वन् को जो (ब्रह्मविद्या) ब्रह्मा ने कही — अथर्वा ने उसे पूर्वकाल में अंगिर (अङ्गिरस्) को कहा। उन्होंने (अंगिर ने) सत्यवाह भारद्वाज को कहा। भारद्वाज ने अंगिरस को (वह) परावरा (higher and lower / पर और अपर — दोनों विद्या) कही।
en: The brahma-vidyā that Brahmā taught to Atharvan — Atharvā in ancient times taught it to Aṅgir. He (Aṅgir) taught it to Satyavāha Bhāradvāja. Bhāradvāja taught to Aṅgiras the parāvarā (the higher and the lower knowledge).

ws.e: to Aṅgir — one of the seven great ṛṣis (saptarṣi); a legendary Vedic sage associated with fire-worship and the Atharvaveda
to Satyavāha Bhāradvāja — satyavāha = 'truth-bearer' (satya + vāha); from the Bharadvāja gotra

ws.h: अंगिरस को / आंगिरस (अंगिर के वंशज) को
ws.e: to Aṅgiras — a descendant of Aṅgir; the sage who will teach Śaunaka in mantra 3; the immediate teacher in this Upanishad

ws.h: पर और अपर (दोनों) विद्या / उच्च और निम्न ज्ञान
ws.e: the higher and the lower (knowledge) — parā (higher) + avarā (lower); the complete knowledge, both aspects; foreshadows the parā/aparā distinction in mantras 4-5

gr: The complete lineage: Brahmā → Atharvā → Aṅgir → Satyavāha Bhāradvāja → Aṅgiras. Five links in the chain, spanning from the Creator to the teacher of this Upanishad. parāvarām — 'the higher and the lower': a compound of parā (higher) and avarā (lower). This single word anticipates the central teaching of this section — the distinction between parā vidyā (higher knowledge = knowledge of Brahman) and aparā vidyā (lower knowledge = the Vedas and auxiliary sciences). The knowledge transmitted is both — the complete package. Two Aṅgirases: the chain mentions both 'Aṅgir' (the ancient ṛṣi, link 3) and 'Aṅgiras' (link 5, the teacher of Śaunaka). They may be the same person or, more likely, ancestor and descendant — the name 'Aṅgiras' meaning 'descendant of Aṅgir.'
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_1.1.2 — The lineage Brahmā → Atharvā → Aṅgir connects the Muṇḍaka firmly to the Atharvaveda tradition. Atharvā and Aṅgir are the two legendary founders of the Atharvaveda (originally called Atharva-Aṅgirasa-Veda). The name Satyavāha ('truth-bearer') may connect to the Satyakāma of the Chāndogya (4.4) and the Prashna (5.1) — though they are likely different individuals. The term 'parāvarā' (higher-and-lower) foreshadows the famous parā/aparā vidyā distinction that is the Muṇḍaka's signature contribution to Vedāntic thought.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'परावरा' = पर विद्या (अक्षर-ज्ञान / ब्रह्म-ज्ञान) और अपर विद्या (वेद-ज्ञान / कर्मकाण्ड-ज्ञान) — दोनों की सम्पूर्ण परम्परा। गुरु-शिष्य श्रृंखला (teacher-student chain) अखण्ड (unbroken) है — ब्रह्मा से लेकर आज तक।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'parāvarā' = parā vidyā (knowledge of the Imperishable / Brahman) and aparā vidyā (Vedic/ritual knowledge) — the complete tradition of both. The guru-student chain is unbroken — from Brahmā to the present.
advaita.ins: The knowledge comes in two parts: the lower (what the world is made of) and the higher (who made it). Both were transmitted together. You need the lower to ask the right questions. You need the higher to find the final answer.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — पाँच-कड़ी (five-link) परम्परा यह सिद्ध करती है कि ब्रह्मविद्या मानव-निर्मित (man-made) नहीं — भगवान् (ब्रह्मा के रूप में) से प्रारम्भ होती है। 'परावरा' = भगवान् के दोनों पक्ष — सगुण (with attributes) और निर्गुण (beyond attributes)।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says the five-link lineage proves brahma-vidyā is not man-made — it originates from the Lord (as Brahmā). 'Parāvarā' = both aspects of the Lord — saguṇa (with attributes) and nirguṇa (beyond attributes).
vishisht.ins: Five teachers, one unbroken chain. Each link trusted the next with the most precious possession — the knowledge of God. That chain reaches you now. Treat it with the same reverence they did.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — ज्ञान-परम्परा = चेतना की अखण्ड धारा (unbroken stream of consciousness) — प्रत्येक गुरु ने अपने शिष्य में चेतना का बीज (seed of consciousness) स्थापित किया। 'परावरा' = अभिव्यक्त (manifest) और अनभिव्यक्त (unmanifest) — सम्पूर्ण ज्ञान।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says the knowledge-lineage = an unbroken stream of consciousness — each teacher planted the seed of consciousness in the student. 'Parāvarā' = manifest and unmanifest — complete knowledge.
aurobindo.ins: Knowledge doesn't travel in books — it travels in people. Each teacher lit a flame in the next student's consciousness. That flame is still burning. The Muṇḍaka's lineage is proof: consciousness can be transmitted.

dp.a: The Muṇḍaka's lineage (Brahmā → Atharvā → Aṅgir) directly connects it to the Atharvaveda: Atharvā and Aṅgir are the two legendary founders of the Atharvaveda, which was originally called the Atharva-Aṅgirasa Veda — the Veda of Atharvan and Aṅgiras. By tracing its lineage through these two figures, the Muṇḍaka claims direct descent from the Atharvaveda's founding teachers. The Atharvaveda's unique position: the Atharvaveda is the fourth Veda — added after the original triad (Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma). It has a different character: while the three older Vedas focus on ritual (yajña), the Atharvaveda includes: (1) Philosophical speculation — many of its Upanishads (Muṇḍaka, Prashna, Māṇḍūkya) are among the most philosophical. (2) Healing and protection — hymns for curing diseases, warding off evil, and ensuring prosperity. (3) Domestic life — charms for love, childbirth, and household welfare. The Muṇḍaka represents the Atharvaveda's philosophical dimension — it is concerned not with rituals or charms but with the highest knowledge (brahma-vidyā). Three Atharvaveda Upanishads: Muṇḍaka, Prashna, and Māṇḍūkya all belong to the Atharvaveda. Together, they cover: Prashna = six questions on cosmology, physiology, and consciousness; Muṇḍaka = the two kinds of knowledge and the path to Brahman; Māṇḍūkya = OM and the four states of consciousness.

The compound parāvarā (पर + अवर = higher + lower) anticipates the Muṇḍaka's central distinction (elaborated in mantras 4-5): Parā vidyā (higher knowledge): the direct knowledge of Brahman — the Imperishable (akṣara), the source of all existence. This knowledge is not information about Brahman but the direct realisation of Brahman. It is what the Muṇḍaka will describe as 'that by which the akṣara is known' (yayā tad akṣaram adhigamyate). Aparā vidyā (lower knowledge): all conventional learning — the four Vedas (Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, Atharva) plus the six Vedāṅgas (phonetics, grammar, metre, etymology, astronomy, ritual procedure). Despite being sacred, this knowledge is called 'lower' because it deals with the phenomenal world — names, forms, rules — rather than with the ground of the phenomenal world. Why transmit both? Because aparā vidyā is the preparation for parā vidyā. You need to understand the rituals, the grammar, the cosmology — not because they are the goal but because they train the mind, purify the heart, and raise the right questions. The student who has mastered aparā vidyā eventually asks: 'Is there something beyond all this?' — and that question opens the door to parā vidyā. The complete teacher (like Aṅgiras) transmits both — the preparation and the goal.

sk: शौनको ह वै महाशालो ऽङ्गिरसं विधिवदुपसन्नः पप्रच्छ कस्मिन्नु भगवो विज्ञाते सर्वमिदं विज्ञातं भवतीति ||
ro: śaunakaḥ · ha · vai · mahā-śālaḥ · aṅgirasaṁ · vidhivat · upasannaḥ · papraccha · kasmin · nu · bhagavaḥ · vijñāte · sarvam · idaṁ · vijñātaṁ · bhavati · iti ||
hi: शौनक — जो महाशाल (great householder / बड़े गृहस्थ) थे — अंगिरस के पास विधिवत् (proper method से) उपसन्न (approached / शिष्य-भाव से आकर) होकर पूछा — 'भगवन्! किसके विज्ञात (known) होने पर यह सब (सर्वम् इदम्) विज्ञात (known) हो जाता है?'
en: Śaunaka, a great householder (mahā-śāla), having duly approached (vidhivat upasannaḥ) Aṅgiras, asked: 'Bhagavan! What is that which, being known (vijñāte), all this (sarvam idam) becomes known?'

ws.e: Śaunaka — the questioner; a great householder (not a renunciant); from the Śunaka lineage; the Muṇḍaka belongs to the Śaunaka school of the Atharvaveda
a great householder — mahā (great) + śālā (hall/house); a wealthy, learned householder; shows that brahma-vidyā is not restricted to renunciants
according to proper procedure — vidhi (rule/method) + vat (having); Śaunaka approached with the proper attitude and formalities of a student seeking a teacher

ws.h: पास आकर / शिष्य-भाव से उपस्थित होकर
ws.e: having approached — upa + √sad (to sit near); the technical term for a student approaching a teacher for instruction; related to 'upaniṣad' (sitting near)

ws.h: जाने जाने पर / विज्ञात होने पर
ws.e: being known — locative absolute of vi + √jñā (to know); 'when X is known'
all this — everything that exists; the entire manifest universe

gr: The great question: 'kasmin vijñāte sarvam idaṁ vijñātaṁ bhavati' — 'What is that, knowing which, all this becomes known?' This is one of the most important questions in the Upanishads. It asks: is there a single knowledge that contains all knowledge? Is there a master-principle whose understanding illuminates everything else? mahā-śāla — 'great householder': Śaunaka is not a wandering ascetic but a prosperous householder — showing that the quest for ultimate knowledge is not restricted to renunciants. Anyone, regardless of social status, can ask the great question. vidhivat upasannaḥ — 'having duly approached': the word upasannaḥ (sitting near) is etymologically related to upaniṣad (the teaching received by sitting near the teacher). Śaunaka followed the proper procedure — approaching with humility, reverence, and genuine desire to learn. The question's structure: it presupposes that such a thing exists — a single knowledge that makes 'all this' known. The answer (mantras 4-6) will be: yes — it is brahma-vidyā, the knowledge of the Imperishable (akṣara).
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_1.1.3 — This is the Muṇḍaka's foundational question — its equivalent of the Prashna's six questions or the Kaṭha's dialogue between Nachiketa and Yama. The question 'kasmin vijñāte sarvam idaṁ vijñātam bhavati' echoes the Chāndogya's (6.1.3) formulation: 'By knowing one lump of clay, all things made of clay are known — the modification being only a name arising from speech, while the truth is that it is clay.' The Bṛhadāraṇyaka (2.4.5, 4.5.6) asks similarly: 'By whose knowledge does one know all this?' The answer there: 'By knowing the Self (ātman), all this is known.' The term 'mahā-śāla' is also used for Janaka in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka — the philosopher-king who sought knowledge while fulfilling his worldly duties.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'कस्मिन् विज्ञाते सर्वम् इदं विज्ञातं भवति' — यह प्रश्न ब्रह्म-ज्ञान की एकतामूलक प्रकृति (unitary nature) को मान्य करता है। जैसे मृत्तिका (clay) जानने से सब मृत्तिका-विकार (clay-products) ज्ञात हो जाते हैं — वैसे ब्रह्म जानने से सर्वज्ञता (omniscience) होती है।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'kasmin vijñāte sarvam idaṁ vijñātaṁ bhavati' — this question presupposes the unitary nature of Brahman-knowledge. As knowing clay makes all clay-products known — so knowing Brahman makes everything known (omniscience).
advaita.ins: One question changes everything: 'Is there one thing, knowing which, I know everything?' If the answer is yes — and the Upanishad says it is — then all our scattered learning is pointing toward one centre. Find the centre, and the circumference takes care of itself.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'सर्वम् इदं विज्ञातं भवति' — भगवान् (ब्रह्म) को जानने से सब ज्ञात होता है क्योंकि भगवान् सबका कारण (cause) और सबका आत्मा (Self) हैं। कारण जानने से कार्य ज्ञात — आत्मा जानने से शरीर ज्ञात।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'sarvam idaṁ vijñātaṁ bhavati' — knowing the Lord (Brahman) makes all known because the Lord is the cause of all and the Self of all. Knowing the cause reveals the effects; knowing the Self reveals the body.
vishisht.ins: Why does knowing God mean knowing everything? Because God is the thread running through all beads. Know the thread, and you understand why every bead is where it is. He's not one thing among many — He's the one thing IN everything.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — शौनक का प्रश्न = चेतना के एकीकरण (unification of consciousness) का प्रश्न। 'एक ज्ञान से सब ज्ञान' — यह तभी सम्भव है जब सम्पूर्ण अस्तित्व एक चेतना (one consciousness) की अभिव्यक्ति हो।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says Śaunaka's question = a question about the unification of consciousness. 'One knowledge = all knowledge' — this is possible only if all existence is the expression of one consciousness.
aurobindo.ins: The question behind the question: is reality unified or fragmented? If one knowledge can illuminate all knowledge, then reality is one. And if reality is one, then what you're looking for isn't far away — it's the very fabric of everything you see.

dp.q: 🔍 The great question: 'knowing which, all is known'
dp.a: Śaunaka's question — 'kasmin vijñāte sarvam idaṁ vijñātaṁ bhavati?' — is the defining question of the Muṇḍaka Upanishad and one of the most important in all of Indian philosophy: What it asks: is there a single piece of knowledge that, once acquired, makes all knowledge accessible? Is there a master-key that opens every lock? Why it's profound: the question assumes that reality has a structure — that the multiplicity of things (trees, rivers, stars, thoughts, emotions) is not a random collection but an expression of a single underlying principle. If you can know that principle, you know the logic behind everything. The clay-pot analogy: the Chāndogya (6.1.4) provides the model: 'By knowing one lump of clay, all things made of clay are known. The modification is a word-name only; the reality is clay.' If Brahman is the 'clay' and the universe is the 'pot,' then knowing Brahman = knowing the universe. Parallel formulations: (1) Chāndogya 6.1.3: 'Have you asked for that instruction by which what has not been heard becomes heard, what has not been thought becomes thought, what has not been known becomes known?' (2) Bṛhadāraṇyaka 2.4.5: 'Indeed, it is not for the sake of the husband that the husband is dear, but for the sake of the Self... the Self is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon. By knowing the Self, all this is known.' The answer (coming in mantras 4-6): the knowledge that makes all known is parā vidyā — the direct knowledge of the Imperishable (akṣara Brahman).

The designation mahā-śāla (great householder) for Śaunaka is significant: Meaning: mahā-śāla = 'one who has a great hall (śālā)' — a wealthy, established householder with a large household, social standing, and worldly success. He is not a renunciant (sannyāsin), not a wandering monk, not an ascetic living in a forest. Why it matters: the Muṇḍaka is demonstrating that the quest for brahma-vidyā is not restricted to renunciants. A householder — someone engaged in the world, with family, property, and social obligations — can and should seek the highest knowledge. This is a recurring Upanishadic theme: (1) Janaka (Bṛhadāraṇyaka): the king of Videha, a philosopher-householder who debated the greatest sages. (2) Satyakāma Jābāla (Chāndogya): a boy of uncertain parentage who sought knowledge purely through truth and integrity. (3) The six seekers of the Prashna: householders who approached Pippalāda. The later tradition's tension: later Vedāntic tradition debated whether liberation (mokṣa) requires renunciation (sannyāsa) or can be achieved by householders (gṛhasthas). Shankara leaned toward renunciation as the ideal; Rāmānuja was more open to the householder path. The Muṇḍaka's 'mahā-śāla' is evidence that the Upanishadic tradition itself did not restrict brahma-vidyā to any one life-stage (āśrama).

sk: तस्मै स होवाच द्वे विद्ये वेदितव्ये इति ह स्म यद्ब्रह्मविदो वदन्ति परा चैवापरा च ||
ro: tasmai · saḥ · ha · uvāca · dve · vidye · veditavye · iti · ha · sma · yat · brahma-vidaḥ · vadanti · parā · ca · eva · aparā · ca ||
hi: उनसे उन्होंने (अंगिरस ने) कहा — 'दो विद्याएँ जानने योग्य (वेदितव्ये) हैं — ऐसा ब्रह्मविद् (ब्रह्मज्ञानी) कहते हैं — परा (higher) और अपरा (lower)।'
en: To him he (Aṅgiras) said: 'Two kinds of knowledge (vidye) are to be known (veditavye) — so say the knowers of Brahman (brahma-vidaḥ) — the higher (parā) and the lower (aparā).'

ws.h: दो विद्याएँ / दो प्रकार के ज्ञान
ws.e: two kinds of knowledge — dual of vidyā; the fundamental epistemological distinction of the Muṇḍaka
to be known — gerundive of √vid (to know); both kinds MUST be known, not just one
the knowers of Brahman — those who have realised Brahman; they are the authority for this classification
the higher — the supreme knowledge; knowledge of Brahman directly
the lower — conventional knowledge; knowledge of the phenomenal world, including the Vedas

gr: The parā/aparā distinction: Aṅgiras begins his answer with a bold classification — all knowledge falls into two categories: parā (higher) and aparā (lower). This is the Muṇḍaka's signature contribution to Vedāntic thought. dve vidye veditavye — 'two knowledges are to be known': note that both must be known (veditavye is dual, matching dve). The Upanishad does not say 'abandon the lower and seek only the higher.' Both have their place. The lower prepares; the higher liberates. brahma-vidaḥ vadanti — 'the knowers of Brahman say': the authority for this classification comes not from scripture or logic but from those who have directly experienced Brahman. They are qualified to distinguish the two kinds of knowledge because they have traversed both. The next mantra will enumerate what falls under 'aparā' — and the answer will be shocking: the four Vedas themselves are classified as 'lower knowledge.'
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_1.1.4 — The parā/aparā vidyā distinction is one of the most cited Vedāntic classifications. It influenced all subsequent Indian epistemology. The Bhagavad Gītā (7.4-5) echoes it with its distinction between aparā prakṛti (the eightfold material nature) and parā prakṛti (the conscious nature). The Yoga Sūtra (1.49) distinguishes śruta-jñāna (knowledge from scripture) from ṛtam-bharā-prajñā (truth-bearing wisdom). The bold move of classifying the Vedas as 'aparā' is what gives the Muṇḍaka its 'razor' reputation — it cuts through conventional reverence to point at the ultimate.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'द्वे विद्ये' — ज्ञान दो प्रकार का है: (1) अपरा = वेद-ज्ञान, कर्मकाण्ड, व्याकरण, ज्योतिष — यह सब 'अविद्या' (ignorance) के अन्तर्गत है — क्योंकि यह नाम-रूप (name-form) से सम्बन्धित है। (2) परा = अक्षर-ब्रह्म-ज्ञान — यही एकमात्र 'विद्या' (true knowledge) है।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'dve vidye' — knowledge is of two kinds: (1) aparā = Vedic knowledge, rituals, grammar, astronomy — all this falls under 'avidyā' (ignorance) because it deals with name-and-form. (2) parā = knowledge of the Imperishable Brahman — this alone is 'vidyā' (true knowledge).
advaita.ins: Two kinds of knowledge: one tells you about the world; the other tells you about the one who made the world. Both are necessary. But only the second one sets you free.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'द्वे विद्ये वेदितव्ये' — दोनों जानने योग्य हैं: अपरा = भगवान् की सृष्टि (creation) का ज्ञान; परा = भगवान् स्वयं का ज्ञान। दोनों भगवान् से सम्बन्धित हैं — अपरा भगवान् के कार्य (work) से, परा भगवान् के स्वरूप (nature) से।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'dve vidye veditavye' — both must be known: aparā = knowledge of the Lord's creation; parā = knowledge of the Lord Himself. Both relate to the Lord — aparā to His work, parā to His nature.
vishisht.ins: There's no such thing as 'secular' and 'sacred' knowledge — both are about God. Science studies God's creation; brahma-vidyā studies God directly. You need both. But don't mistake the map for the territory.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'द्वे विद्ये' = दो ज्ञान-स्तर: अपरा = बाह्य/विश्लेषणात्मक ज्ञान (external/analytical knowledge) — विज्ञान, दर्शन, धर्मशास्त्र; परा = आन्तरिक/अनुभवात्मक ज्ञान (internal/experiential knowledge) — ब्रह्म-साक्षात्कार।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'dve vidye' = two levels of knowledge: aparā = external/analytical knowledge — science, philosophy, theology; parā = internal/experiential knowledge — direct Brahman-realisation.
aurobindo.ins: You can study light with instruments — that's aparā. Or you can become light — that's parā. The Upanishad says: do both. Study the world. Then transcend the study and become what you were studying.

dp.q: 🔍 The parā/aparā distinction — the Muṇḍaka's central teaching
dp.a: The distinction between parā vidyā (higher knowledge) and aparā vidyā (lower knowledge) is the signature contribution of the Muṇḍaka Upanishad to Indian philosophy: What makes this distinction revolutionary? It classifies the Vedas themselves — the most sacred texts in the Hindu tradition — as lower knowledge. This is not disrespectful but perspectival: the Vedas are 'lower' not because they are wrong but because they deal with the phenomenal world (creation, rituals, duties) rather than with the ground of the phenomenal world (Brahman). The logic: (1) All conventional knowledge (aparā) deals with objects — things that can be named, described, and categorised. (2) Brahman is not an object — it is the subject, the knower, the ground of all objects. (3) Therefore, Brahman cannot be known by any knowledge that deals with objects. A different kind of knowledge (parā) is needed — not information about Brahman but the direct realisation of Brahman. Both are necessary: the Upanishad says 'dve vidye veditavye' — both must be known. Aparā is the preparation; parā is the goal. You cannot skip the preparation (as the next mantra makes clear, aparā includes the Vedas — the very texts that contain the Upanishads). But you must not stop at the preparation.

dp.q: 🔍 Why do the 'knowers of Brahman' (brahma-vidaḥ) make this distinction?
dp.a: The text says brahma-vidaḥ vadanti — 'the knowers of Brahman say' this. The authority for the parā/aparā distinction comes not from scripture or logical argument but from those who have directly experienced Brahman: Why their testimony matters: only someone who has been to the far shore can tell you that the near shore is 'lower' and the far shore is 'higher.' Someone standing on the near shore can't make this distinction — they don't know what the far shore looks like. The brahma-vid (knower of Brahman) has traversed both domains — he has mastered aparā vidyā (the Vedas, grammar, etc.) and then gone beyond it to parā vidyā (direct Brahman-realisation). From that vantage point, he can see the relationship between the two. The qualification: this is not a claim that aparā vidyā is useless — the brahma-vid himself went through it. It is a claim that aparā vidyā is insufficient by itself. A ladder is essential for reaching the roof, but once on the roof, you don't need the ladder. The brahma-vid is on the roof; he can see both the ladder (aparā) and the view (parā). The implication for the student: don't reject the Vedas — study them. But don't stop there. The Vedas themselves point beyond themselves to the akṣara (Imperishable) that no Veda can capture in words.

sk: तत्रापरा ऋग्वेदो यजुर्वेदः सामवेदो ऽथर्ववेदः शिक्षा कल्पो व्याकरणं निरुक्तं छन्दो ज्योतिषमिति अथ परा यया तदक्षरमधिगम्यते ||
ro: tatra · aparā · ṛg-vedaḥ · yajur-vedaḥ · sāma-vedaḥ · atharva-vedaḥ · śikṣā · kalpaḥ · vyākaraṇaṁ · niruktaṁ · chandaḥ · jyotiṣam · iti · atha · parā · yayā · tat · akṣaram · adhigamyate ||
hi: उनमें अपरा (lower knowledge) है — ऋग्वेद, यजुर्वेद, सामवेद, अथर्ववेद, शिक्षा (phonetics), कल्प (ritual procedure), व्याकरण (grammar), निरुक्त (etymology), छन्दस् (metre), और ज्योतिष (astronomy)। और परा (higher knowledge) वह है — जिससे उस अक्षर (Imperishable) को अधिगम्य (attained / known) किया जाता है।
en: Of these, the lower (aparā) is: the Ṛg Veda, the Yajur Veda, the Sāma Veda, the Atharva Veda, phonetics (śikṣā), ritual procedure (kalpa), grammar (vyākaraṇa), etymology (nirukta), metre (chandas), and astronomy (jyotiṣa). And the higher (parā) is that by which the Imperishable (akṣara) is attained (adhigamyate).

ws.e: phonetics — the science of correct pronunciation of Vedic syllables; the first of the six Vedāṅgas (limbs of the Veda)
ritual procedure — the rules for performing Vedic sacrifices; the Śrauta and Gṛhya Sūtras belong to this Vedāṅga
grammar — the analysis of language; Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī is the supreme achievement of this Vedāṅga
etymology — the derivation and explanation of Vedic words; Yāska's Nirukta is the foundational text
metre — the study of Vedic metres (gāyatrī, triṣṭubh, jagatī, etc.); Piṅgala's Chandaḥśāstra is the key text
astronomy/astrology — the science of celestial bodies; used to determine the correct times for Vedic rituals
the Imperishable — a (not) + kṣara (perishable); Brahman as the indestructible ground of all existence; the object of parā vidyā

gr: Aparā vidyā enumerated: ten items — the four Vedas plus the six Vedāṅgas (auxiliary sciences). This is the entire corpus of conventional sacred learning. The four Vedas: Ṛg (hymns), Yajur (ritual formulae), Sāma (chants), Atharva (incantations and philosophy). The six Vedāṅgas: (1) Śikṣā (phonetics), (2) Kalpa (ritual), (3) Vyākaraṇa (grammar), (4) Nirukta (etymology), (5) Chandas (metre), (6) Jyotiṣa (astronomy). Together, these constitute the complete 'curriculum' of Vedic education. The shock: the Vedas — the holiest texts — are classified as lower knowledge. This does not mean they are false or useless, but that they deal with the manifest world (rituals, duties, cosmic order) rather than with the source of the manifest world. parā yayā tad akṣaram adhigamyate — 'the higher is that by which the Imperishable is attained': parā vidyā is defined by its object — the akṣara (Imperishable Brahman). It is not a text or a technique but the direct realisation of the Imperishable. Note: adhigamyate = 'is attained/reached' — not just 'known about.' Parā vidyā is experiential, not informational.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_1.1.5 — This is the Muṇḍaka's most famous mantra — the explicit classification of the four Vedas as aparā vidyā. This was revolutionary in its time and remains one of the boldest statements in Indian philosophy. The six Vedāṅgas listed here are the standard enumeration found in the Pāṇinīya Śikṣā (41-42). The term 'akṣara' (imperishable) for Brahman is characteristic of the Muṇḍaka — it will appear repeatedly throughout the text (cf. 1.1.6, 2.1.2, 2.2.2). The Bhagavad Gītā (8.3, 15.16-18) and the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (3.8.8-11) also use 'akṣara' as a primary name for Brahman.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — चारों वेद और छह वेदाङ्ग 'अपरा' हैं — क्योंकि ये सब अनात्मविषयक (non-Self-related) ज्ञान हैं — नाम-रूप-कर्म (name, form, action) से सम्बन्धित। 'अक्षरम्' = निर्गुण ब्रह्म — जो नाम-रूप से परे है। परा विद्या = अक्षर-ब्रह्म का साक्षात्कार।
advaita.en: Shankara says the four Vedas and six Vedāṅgas are 'aparā' because they concern non-Self-related knowledge — dealing with name, form, and action. 'Akṣara' = nirguṇa Brahman — beyond name and form. Parā vidyā = the direct realisation of the imperishable Brahman.
advaita.ins: The Vedas are sacred — but they're still words about things. Parā vidyā is not words about Brahman; it's Brahman knowing itself through you. The difference is not between good and bad knowledge but between the map and the territory.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — अपरा = वेद-वेदाङ्ग — ये भगवान् की उपासना (worship) और कर्तव्य (duty) का मार्ग बताते हैं। परा = भगवान् का स्वरूप-ज्ञान (essential-nature-knowledge) — 'अक्षर' = भगवान् का अविनाशी स्वरूप।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says aparā = Vedas and Vedāṅgas — they teach the path of worship and duty toward the Lord. Parā = knowledge of the Lord's essential nature. 'Akṣara' = the Lord's imperishable nature.
vishisht.ins: The Vedas teach you how to worship God. Parā vidyā teaches you who God actually is. Both are necessary — you can't worship someone you don't know, and you can't know someone you've never approached.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — अपरा विद्या = बाह्य ज्ञान-प्रणाली (external knowledge-systems) — वैज्ञानिक, दार्शनिक, धार्मिक। परा विद्या = आन्तरिक अनुभव (inner experience) — 'अक्षर' = शाश्वत चेतना (eternal consciousness) का प्रत्यक्ष ज्ञान।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says aparā vidyā = external knowledge-systems — scientific, philosophical, religious. Parā vidyā = inner experience — 'akṣara' = direct knowledge of eternal consciousness.
aurobindo.ins: You can read every book ever written — Vedas, sciences, philosophies — and still not know the Imperishable. Because the Imperishable is not in any book. It's in you. Books point; parā vidyā arrives.

dp.q: 🔍 The four Vedas and six Vedāṅgas
dp.a: The ten components of aparā vidyā constitute the complete curriculum of traditional Vedic education: The four Vedas: (1) Ṛg Veda — hymns of praise (ṛc); the oldest Veda; contains ~10,600 verses addressed to various deities. (2) Yajur Veda — sacrificial formulae (yajus); the manual for performing rituals; exists in two recensions (Śukla/White and Kṛṣṇa/Black). (3) Sāma Veda — melodies (sāman); the Vedic hymns set to music; the 'song-book' of the priests. (4) Atharva Veda — incantations and philosophy; the fourth Veda, named after the sage Atharvan; includes both practical charms and deep philosophical Upanishads (Muṇḍaka, Prashna, Māṇḍūkya). The six Vedāṅgas ('limbs of the Veda'): (1) Śikṣā (phonetics) — correct pronunciation of Vedic syllables; precision of sound is essential because Vedic mantras derive their power from exact phonetic reproduction. (2) Kalpa (ritual procedure) — the rules for performing sacrifices (Śrauta Sūtras), domestic rites (Gṛhya Sūtras), and dharmic conduct (Dharma Sūtras). (3) Vyākaraṇa (grammar) — the analysis of Sanskrit; Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī is the crowning achievement. (4) Nirukta (etymology) — the derivation and meaning of Vedic words; Yāska's Nirukta is the foundational text. (5) Chandas (metre) — the study of poetic metres used in Vedic composition. (6) Jyotiṣa (astronomy) — determining the correct astronomical conditions for performing rituals. All ten are 'aparā': despite their sacredness, all ten deal with the phenomenal world — words, sounds, rituals, times, rules. None of them, by themselves, can reveal the akṣara (Imperishable).

The word akṣara (अक्षर) is the Muṇḍaka's primary name for Brahman. It means 'the Imperishable' — that which does not perish (a + kṣara): Etymology: a (not) + kṣara (perishable/decaying), from √kṣar (to flow away/perish). The akṣara is that which never flows away — the unchanging ground beneath all change. Double meaning: 'akṣara' also means 'syllable' (the basic unit of speech that cannot be further divided). The most akṣara of all akṣaras is OM — the imperishable syllable. The Bhagavad Gītā (8.13) identifies them: 'om ity ekākṣaraṁ brahma' — 'OM, the single syllable, is Brahman.' The akṣara in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (3.8.8-11): Gārgī asks Yājñavalkya: 'What is the akṣara?' He replies with a famous via-negativa description: 'It is not gross, not subtle, not short, not long, not red, not sticky, not shadowy, not dark, not air, not space, without attachment, without taste, without smell, without eyes, without ears, without speech, without mind, without light, without breath, without mouth, without measure, without inside, without outside. It consumes nothing, and no one consumes it.' Parā vidyā's object: the akṣara is what parā vidyā 'attains' (adhigamyate). Not 'learns about' but attains — direct, experiential, transformative knowledge. This is not information but identity: the knower becomes the akṣara (Muṇḍaka 3.2.9: 'brahma-vid brahmaiva bhavati' — 'the knower of Brahman becomes Brahman').

sk: यत्तदद्रेश्यमग्राह्यमगोत्रमवर्णमचक्षुःश्रोत्रं तदपाणिपादम् नित्यं विभुं सर्वगतं सुसूक्ष्मं तदव्ययं यद्भूतयोनिं परिपश्यन्ति धीराः ||
ro: yat · tat · adreśyam · agrāhyam · agotram · avarṇam · acakṣuḥ-śrotram · tat · apāṇi-pādam · nityaṁ · vibhuṁ · sarvagataṁ · susūkṣmaṁ · tat · avyayaṁ · yat · bhūta-yoniṁ · paripaśyanti · dhīrāḥ ||
hi: जो वह (अक्षर ब्रह्म) अदृश्य (invisible) है, अग्राह्य (ungraspable) है, अगोत्र (without lineage) है, अवर्ण (without colour/caste) है, बिना नेत्रों (acakṣuḥ) और बिना कानों (aśrotra) वाला है, बिना हाथों (apāṇi) और बिना पैरों (apāda) वाला है — नित्य (eternal), विभु (all-pervading), सर्वगत (omnipresent), सुसूक्ष्म (supremely subtle) — वह अव्यय (imperishable) है — जिसे धीर (wise) पुरुष सब भूतों (beings) के योनि (source) के रूप में सर्वत्र देखते (परिपश्यन्ति) हैं।
en: That which is invisible (adreśya), ungraspable (agrāhya), without lineage (agotra), without colour (avarṇa), without eyes or ears (acakṣuḥ-śrotra), without hands or feet (apāṇi-pāda) — eternal (nitya), all-pervading (vibhu), omnipresent (sarvagata), supremely subtle (susūkṣma) — that imperishable (avyaya) which the wise (dhīrāḥ) see everywhere as the source of all beings (bhūta-yoni).

ws.e: invisible — a + dṛśya (visible); cannot be seen by the physical eyes; beyond the range of sensory perception
ungraspable — a + grāhya (graspable); cannot be seized by the hands or grasped by the mind as an object
without lineage/clan — a + gotra; Brahman has no family, no ancestry, no genealogy; it is uncreated
without colour or caste — a + varṇa; Brahman has no colour (not perceivable) and no social classification
the source/womb of all beings — bhūta (beings) + yoni (womb/source); Brahman is the origin from which all creatures emerge
the wise / the steady-minded — from √dhī (to think/perceive); those with mature spiritual insight who can 'see' what ordinary perception cannot

gr: Via-negativa description of Brahman: this mantra describes the akṣara through a series of negations — what it is not. This is the classic Upanishadic method (neti neti — 'not this, not this'): since Brahman transcends all categories, it can only be described by negating categories. Eight negations: (1) adreśya (invisible), (2) agrāhya (ungraspable), (3) agotra (without lineage), (4) avarṇa (without colour/caste), (5) acakṣuḥ (without eyes), (6) aśrotra (without ears), (7) apāṇi (without hands), (8) apāda (without feet). Five positive attributes: (1) nitya (eternal), (2) vibhu (all-pervading), (3) sarvagata (omnipresent), (4) susūkṣma (supremely subtle), (5) avyaya (imperishable). bhūta-yonim paripaśyanti dhīrāḥ — 'the wise see it everywhere as the source of all beings': despite being invisible and ungraspable, the akṣara is seen (paripaśyanti = 'see all around') by the wise — not with physical eyes but with the eye of knowledge (jñāna-cakṣu). They see it as the bhūta-yoni — the womb/source from which all beings arise.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_1.1.6 — This via-negativa description closely parallels the Śvetāśvatara (3.19): 'apāṇi-pādo javano grahītā paśyaty acakṣuḥ sa śṛṇoty akarṇaḥ' — 'Without hands or feet, He is swift and seizing; He sees without eyes, hears without ears.' The Bṛhadāraṇyaka (3.8.8) has a more extended via-negativa for the akṣara. The term 'bhūta-yoni' (source of all beings) recurs in the Bhagavad Gītā (14.3): 'mama yonir mahad brahma tasmin garbhaṁ dadhāmy aham' — 'My womb is the great Brahman; in that I place the germ.' The paradox of 'without eyes yet seeing, without feet yet moving' is central to the Upanishadic understanding: Brahman transcends the organs but possesses their functions in a transcendent mode.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — आठ निषेध (negations) यह सिद्ध करते हैं कि ब्रह्म किसी भी सांसारिक कोटि (worldly category) में नहीं आता — न दृश्य, न ग्राह्य, न सवर्ण, न सगोत्र, न सेन्द्रिय (with organs)। 'भूतयोनि' — फिर भी सब भूतों का कारण (cause) है — निर्गुण (attributeless) होते हुए भी सगुण (attributed) जगत् का स्रोत है।
advaita.en: Shankara says the eight negations prove Brahman doesn't fall into any worldly category — not visible, not graspable, without colour, lineage, or organs. 'Bhūta-yoni' — yet it is the cause of all beings — attributeless yet the source of the attributed world.
advaita.ins: You can't see it, touch it, classify it, or locate it. It has no eyes, no ears, no hands, no feet. And yet — it sees, hears, acts, and moves through everything. It is the source of all beings — invisible, but the cause of everything visible.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — निषेध (negations) का अर्थ यह नहीं कि भगवान् शून्य (void) हैं — बल्कि भगवान् के गुण प्राकृत (material) नहीं हैं। 'अचक्षुः' = प्राकृत नेत्र नहीं — किन्तु दिव्य दृष्टि (divine vision) है। 'भूतयोनि' = सब जीवों के जनक (father) और पालक (sustainer)।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says the negations don't mean the Lord is void — they mean His attributes are not material. 'Acakṣuḥ' = no material eyes — but He has divine vision. 'Bhūta-yoni' = the father and sustainer of all beings.
vishisht.ins: When the Upanishad says 'without eyes,' it doesn't mean blind. It means: His sight is not limited to two small organs on a face. He sees everything, everywhere, always — with a vision that has no instrument and no limit.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'नेति-नेति' वर्णन = चेतना की अन्तिम सत्ता (ultimate reality of consciousness) — जो सब उपाधियों (limiting adjuncts) से परे है। 'धीराः परिपश्यन्ति' — विवेकी पुरुष इसे सर्वत्र भूतयोनि (source of all beings) के रूप में 'देखते' हैं — ज्ञान-दृष्टि (knowledge-vision) से, न कि चर्म-चक्षु (physical eyes) से।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says the 'neti-neti' description = the ultimate reality of consciousness — beyond all limiting adjuncts. 'Dhīrāḥ paripaśyanti' — the wise 'see' it everywhere as the source of all beings — with knowledge-vision, not physical eyes.
aurobindo.ins: The Imperishable has no form — but forms come from it. It has no colour — but colours come from it. It has no sound — but sounds come from it. It's not nothing — it's the everything from which all things emerge. The wise see this. Everyone else sees only the things.

dp.a: This mantra employs the via-negativa (निषेध-विधि / neti neti method) — describing Brahman by saying what it is not: Why negation? Because Brahman is infinite. Any positive description ('Brahman is X') would limit Brahman — if Brahman is X, then it is not non-X, which makes it finite. By negating all categories, the Upanishad points to something that transcends all categories. The eight negations: (1) Adreśya — not visible → Brahman is not an object of sight. (2) Agrāhya — not graspable → Brahman is not an object that can be seized (physically or conceptually). (3) Agotra — without lineage → Brahman is not born into a family; it has no origin. (4) Avarṇa — without colour or caste → Brahman cannot be classified. (5-6) Acakṣuḥ-śrotra — without eyes or ears → Brahman has no sense-organs (yet it perceives). (7-8) Apāṇi-pāda — without hands or feet → Brahman has no motor-organs (yet it acts). The paradox: the Śvetāśvatara (3.19) resolves the paradox: 'Without hands, He grasps; without feet, He moves; without eyes, He sees.' Brahman transcends the organs but possesses the functions of the organs in a transcendent mode. It is not less than a being with organs but more — it has the capacities without the limitations. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka's extended version (3.8.8): Yājñavalkya's famous description of the akṣara adds even more negations: 'not gross, not subtle, not short, not long, not red, not sticky...' — a comprehensive demolition of every possible category the mind might try to apply.

The compound bhūta-yoni (भूतयोनि) is one of the Muṇḍaka's key terms for Brahman: Meaning: bhūta (beings/elements) + yoni (womb/source/origin). Brahman is the womb from which all beings are born — the universal source, the primordial matrix. Dual significance: (1) Cosmological: Brahman is the source of the five elements (bhūtas — earth, water, fire, air, space) and all beings made of those elements. (2) Ontological: Brahman is the ground of being — every entity exists because Brahman sustains it; remove Brahman, and nothing remains. The paradox with via-negativa: the same Brahman that is 'invisible, ungraspable, without eyes or ears' is also the 'source of all beings.' How can something that has no qualities produce everything with qualities? The Advaita answer: through māyā (the mysterious creative power). The Vishishtadvaita answer: through divine will (saṅkalpa). Sri Aurobindo's answer: through self-manifestation — consciousness expressing itself at progressively denser levels. Parallels: the Bhagavad Gītā (14.3) uses the same image: 'mama yonir mahad brahma' — 'My womb is the great Brahman.' The Taittirīya (3.1.1) provides another formulation: 'yato vā imāni bhūtāni jāyante' — 'That from which these beings are born.'

sk: यथोर्णनाभिः सृजते गृह्णते च यथा पृथिव्यामोषधयः सम्भवन्ति यथा सतः पुरुषात्केशलोमानि तथाक्षरात्सम्भवतीह विश्वम् ||
ro: yathā · ūrṇa-nābhiḥ · sṛjate · gṛhṇate · ca · yathā · pṛthivyām · oṣadhayaḥ · sambhavanti · yathā · sataḥ · puruṣāt · keśa-lomāni · tathā · akṣarāt · sambhavati · iha · viśvam ||
hi: जैसे मकड़ी (ऊर्णनाभि) (जाला) सृजती है और (वापस) ग्रहण करती है; जैसे पृथ्वी पर औषधियाँ (वनस्पतियाँ) उत्पन्न होती हैं; जैसे जीवित पुरुष (व्यक्ति) से केश (सिर के बाल) और लोम (शरीर के रोम) उत्पन्न होते हैं — वैसे ही अक्षर (Imperishable) से यहाँ (इस लोक में) विश्व (universe) उत्पन्न होता है।
en: As a spider (ūrṇa-nābhi) projects and withdraws (its web); as herbs (oṣadhayaḥ) spring up on the earth; as hair (keśa-lomāni) grows from a living person — so from the Imperishable (akṣara) arises here the universe (viśva).

ws.h: मकड़ी (ऊन-नाभि = जिसकी नाभि से ऊन/धागा निकलता है)
ws.e: a spider — ūrṇa (wool/thread) + nābhi (navel); the spider that projects its web from within itself and reabsorbs it; a model for Brahman as both efficient and material cause

ws.h: सृजन करती है और ग्रहण करती है / बनाती है और वापस लेती है
ws.e: projects and withdraws — √sṛj (to emit) + √grah (to seize/take back); the spider both creates and re-absorbs its web
herbs / plants — they spring up from the earth spontaneously; the earth doesn't lose anything by producing them

ws.h: केश (सिर के बाल) और लोम (शरीर के रोम)
ws.e: hair of the head and body — they grow from a living person without effort or loss; the person doesn't become less by growing hair

gr: Three similes for creation: (1) Spider-web (ūrṇa-nābhi): the spider emits its web from within itself — the web's material is the spider's own body. It also re-absorbs the web. This illustrates Brahman as both the efficient cause (the maker) and the material cause (the material) of the universe — and the universe's eventual re-absorption into Brahman. (2) Earth-herbs (pṛthivī-oṣadhi): herbs grow from the earth spontaneously and naturally. The earth doesn't 'try' to produce them — they emerge from its nature. Similarly, the universe emerges from Brahman naturally, without effort. (3) Person-hair (puruṣa-keśa): hair grows from a living person without the person's conscious effort and without diminishing the person. Similarly, the universe grows from Brahman without effort and without diminishing Brahman. Key insight: all three similes show creation as a natural emanation — not a deliberate construction (like a potter making a pot) but a spontaneous expression of the source's own nature.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_1.1.7 — The spider-web simile is one of the most famous in the Upanishads. It appears also in Bṛhadāraṇyaka 2.1.20: 'yathā ūrṇa-nābhiḥ tantunā uccaret' — 'as a spider goes up by its thread.' The Śvetāśvatara (6.10) uses it for God's creative power. The three similes together illustrate three aspects of creation: (1) Spider = creation and re-absorption (sṛṣṭi and pralaya); (2) Earth-herbs = spontaneous, effortless emanation; (3) Hair = creation without diminution of the source. The Bhagavad Gītā (9.4-5) echoes the hair-simile: 'All beings exist in Me, but I am not in them... My Self sustains all beings but does not dwell in them.'

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — मकड़ी-उपमा सर्वोत्तम है — मकड़ी जाले का उपादान कारण (material cause) भी है और निमित्त कारण (efficient cause) भी। वैसे ही ब्रह्म विश्व का — दोनों कारण (both causes) है। सृष्टि = ब्रह्म से प्रक्षेपण (projection); प्रलय = ब्रह्म में पुनः ग्रहण (re-absorption)।
advaita.en: Shankara says the spider-simile is supreme — the spider is both the material cause and the efficient cause of its web. Similarly, Brahman is both causes of the universe. Creation = projection from Brahman; dissolution = re-absorption into Brahman.
advaita.ins: The spider doesn't fetch thread from outside — the thread comes from its own body. It doesn't hire a weaver — it weaves itself. And when it's done, it eats the web and takes the thread back in. Brahman creates the universe exactly like this — from itself, by itself, and back into itself.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — तीन उपमाएँ तीन पक्ष दिखाती हैं: मकड़ी = सृष्टि और प्रलय (creation and dissolution); पृथ्वी-औषधि = सहज-स्वाभाविक सृष्टि (spontaneous creation); केश-लोम = बिना ह्रास (without diminution) के सृष्टि। भगवान् अनन्त (infinite) रहते हुए अनन्त विश्व को सृजते हैं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says the three similes show three aspects: spider = creation and dissolution; earth-herbs = spontaneous creation; hair = creation without diminution. The Lord creates an infinite universe while remaining infinite.
vishisht.ins: Three images, one truth: the universe comes from God the way a web comes from a spider, herbs from the earth, hair from a person. Naturally. Effortlessly. Without the source losing anything.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — तीन उपमाएँ चेतना के आत्म-प्रकटीकरण (self-manifestation) के तीन मॉडल हैं: (1) मकड़ी = सचेतन सृजन और पुनर्ग्रहण; (2) पृथ्वी-औषधि = प्रकृति (Nature) की सहज उत्पादकता; (3) केश = बिना प्रयास, बिना ह्रास — शाश्वत उत्सर्जन (eternal emanation)।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says the three similes are three models of consciousness's self-manifestation: (1) spider = conscious creation and re-absorption; (2) earth-herbs = Nature's spontaneous productivity; (3) hair = effortless, loss-less, eternal emanation.
aurobindo.ins: Creation isn't a factory operation — it's a natural overflow. The spider weaves from its own substance. The earth sprouts herbs without trying. Hair grows while you sleep. The universe emerges from the Imperishable the same way — naturally, effortlessly, endlessly.

dp.a: The spider-web simile (ūrṇanābhi-upamā) is one of the most important analogies for creation in Indian philosophy: The image: a spider emits its web from within its own body (the silk comes from internal glands), dwells in the web it has created, and eventually re-absorbs the web back into itself. What it teaches about Brahman's creation: (1) Brahman is both the efficient and material cause: the spider is both the weaver (efficient cause) and the thread (material cause). Brahman doesn't create from external material — it creates from itself. (2) Creation is not separate from the creator: the web is not 'other' than the spider — it is the spider's own substance extended outward. Similarly, the universe is not 'other' than Brahman — it is Brahman's own nature expressed as multiplicity. (3) Creation is reversible: the spider can re-absorb the web. Similarly, Brahman can dissolve the universe back into itself (pralaya). This cycle of emission and re-absorption is endless. (4) The creator is not diminished by creating: the spider doesn't become less by spinning a web — it remains fully a spider. Similarly, Brahman is not diminished by creating the universe (pūrṇam adaḥ pūrṇam idam — 'that is full, this is full'; Īśā Invocation). The simile's limitations: the spider creates unconsciously (by instinct), whereas Brahman creates consciously (sa aikṣata — 'He saw/willed'). Also, the spider's web is external to the spider's body, whereas the universe is never truly external to Brahman.

This mantra presents three complementary similes for how the universe arises from the Imperishable: (1) Spider and web — CONSCIOUS CREATION + RE-ABSORPTION: The spider chooses to spin (or at least acts from its own nature), and it takes back what it created. Model: creation as a conscious, reversible act. The universe is emitted from Brahman and will eventually be reabsorbed. Key insight: the creator and the creation are made of the same substance. (2) Earth and herbs — SPONTANEOUS EMANATION: Herbs spring up from the earth without effort — the earth doesn't 'try' to produce them. They grow by the earth's inherent nature. Model: creation as natural, effortless self-expression. Key insight: creation is not laborious — it flows from Brahman's nature as naturally as grass grows from soil. (3) Person and hair — LOSS-LESS GROWTH: Hair grows from a living person without diminishing the person and without conscious effort. The person doesn't become smaller or weaker by growing hair. Model: creation as emanation that doesn't diminish the source. Key insight: the Imperishable remains full (pūrṇa) even after creating the universe — it is not 'used up' by creation. Together: the three similes teach that creation is (1) from Brahman's own substance (spider), (2) natural and effortless (earth-herbs), and (3) without any loss to Brahman (hair). No single simile captures the whole truth — but together they give a rich picture of Brahman's creative act.

sk: तपसा चीयते ब्रह्म ततो ऽन्नमभिजायते अन्नात्प्राणो मनः सत्यं लोकाः कर्मसु चामृतम् ||
ro: tapasā · cīyate · brahma · tataḥ · annam · abhijāyate · annāt · prāṇaḥ · manaḥ · satyaṁ · lokāḥ · karmasu · ca · amṛtam ||
hi: तप (tapas) से ब्रह्म बढ़ता है (चीयते / grows / expands)। उससे अन्न (food / matter) उत्पन्न होता है। अन्न से — प्राण (life-force), मन (mind), सत्य (truth / the real elements), लोक (worlds) — और कर्मों में अमृत (the immortal fruit of action) — (ये सब उत्पन्न होते हैं)।
en: By tapas (creative heat), Brahman swells (cīyate). From it, food (anna) is born. From food — prāṇa (life-force), mind (manas), truth (satya, the real elements), the worlds (lokāḥ) — and in actions, immortality (amṛta).

ws.e: by tapas — creative heat / austerity; here, the primordial creative energy by which Brahman 'expands' into creation; tapas is the engine of manifestation

ws.h: बढ़ता है / विस्तृत होता है / संचित होता है
ws.e: swells / grows / is built up — √ci (to gather/build); Brahman 'builds up' or 'expands' through tapas; the image is of a fire being stoked (tapas = heat)
truth / the real elements — here, the five true (real) elements: earth, water, fire, air, space; the 'true' building-blocks of the physical world

ws.h: कर्मों में अमृतत्व / कर्म-फल में अमरता
ws.e: immortality in actions — the immortal fruit embedded within the rituals and righteous actions; the link between karma and its imperishable results

gr: The cosmogonic sequence: Brahman → (through tapas) → anna (food/matter) → prāṇa (life) → manas (mind) → satya (elements) → lokāḥ (worlds) → amṛta in karma (immortality through action). This is a compact creation-account moving from the subtlest (Brahman's tapas) to the grossest (worlds) and back to the transcendent (amṛta). tapasā cīyate brahma — 'by tapas, Brahman swells': tapas here is not human austerity but the primordial creative heat — the energy of self-manifestation. Brahman 'builds itself up' (cīyate, from √ci — to pile up, as in building a fire-altar) through this inner heat, and from that expansion, creation flows. karmasu amṛtam — 'immortality in actions': a striking phrase. Even within the world of karma (action, ritual, duty), there is a seed of immortality — the imperishable fruit of righteous action. This connects aparā vidyā (action/ritual) to parā vidyā (immortality) — even the 'lower' knowledge contains a pointer to the 'higher.'
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_1.1.8 — The sequence Brahman → tapas → anna → prāṇa → manas echoes the Taittirīya's creation-account (2.1): 'From this Self (ātman), space arose; from space, air; from air, fire; from fire, water; from water, earth; from earth, herbs; from herbs, food; from food, the person.' The Muṇḍaka's version is more compact and adds the cultural dimension (karma, amṛta). The phrase 'tapasā cīyate brahma' may refer to the cosmic tapas of Prajāpati described in Aitareya 1.1.1 and Taittirīya 2.6.1. The term 'cīyate' (is built up/piled) may allude to the Vedic fire-altar construction (agnicayana), where the altar is 'piled up' (cīyate) brick by brick — creation as the 'building' of the cosmic altar.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'तपसा चीयते ब्रह्म' — तपस् = ज्ञान-शक्ति (knowledge-power) — जिससे ब्रह्म (सगुण/अपर ब्रह्म) प्रकट होता है और सृष्टि का विस्तार होता है। अन्न → प्राण → मनः — यह सृष्टि-क्रम (creation-sequence) है। 'कर्मसु अमृतम्' — कर्मों में भी अमृतत्व का बीज है — किन्तु यह ज्ञान (knowledge) के बिना अपूर्ण है।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'tapasā cīyate brahma' — tapas = knowledge-power by which Brahman (saguṇa/apara Brahman) manifests and creation expands. Anna → prāṇa → manas = the creation-sequence. 'Karmasu amṛtam' — even actions contain a seed of immortality — but without knowledge, it is incomplete.
advaita.ins: Brahman doesn't create coldly — it creates with heat, with intensity, with tapas. That creative fire is still burning. Everything you see — food, breath, mind, worlds — is that fire's product. And hidden in every action you perform is a seed of immortality.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'तपसा चीयते' — भगवान् का तपस् = दिव्य संकल्प (divine will)। इस संकल्प से सृष्टि का विस्तार होता है — अन्न, प्राण, मन, लोक। 'कर्मसु अमृतम्' — भगवान् के प्रति समर्पित कर्म (dedicated action) अमृतत्व (immortality) देता है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'tapasā cīyate' — the Lord's tapas = divine will. Through this will, creation expands — food, prāṇa, mind, worlds. 'Karmasu amṛtam' — action dedicated to the Lord yields immortality.
vishisht.ins: God's creative heat is His divine will — it builds the universe layer by layer: matter, life, mind, worlds. And woven into the fabric of action itself is a thread of immortality — if you offer the action to God.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'तपसा चीयते ब्रह्म' — चेतना (consciousness) अपनी ऊर्जा (tapas) से स्वयं को विस्तृत (expand) करती है — सृष्टि = चेतना का क्रमिक अवरोहण (progressive descent): अन्न (matter) → प्राण (life) → मन (mind) → लोक (worlds)। 'कर्मसु अमृतम्' — क्रिया (action) में भी शाश्वत (eternal) तत्त्व निहित है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'tapasā cīyate brahma' — consciousness expands itself through its own energy (tapas). Creation = progressive descent of consciousness: anna (matter) → prāṇa (life) → manas (mind) → lokāḥ (worlds). 'Karmasu amṛtam' — even action contains an eternal element.
aurobindo.ins: Consciousness doesn't just sit there — it burns, it heats, it builds. Through tapas, it constructs the universe: first matter, then life, then mind, then worlds. And in every action performed in those worlds, there's a spark of the immortal — if you know how to find it.

dp.q: 🔍 Tapas as the engine of creation
dp.a: The phrase tapasā cīyate brahma ('by tapas, Brahman swells/expands') presents tapas as the engine of creation: What is tapas? The word tapas comes from √tap (to heat/burn). It has multiple levels of meaning: (1) Physical heat: the primordial heat that initiates cosmic processes (like the Big Bang's initial energy). (2) Creative intensity: the concentrated energy of will by which Brahman 'decides' to manifest as the universe. (3) Spiritual austerity: in the human context, tapas is the disciplined intensity of meditation, fasting, or other practices that generate transformative 'heat.' Tapas in the creation-accounts: (1) Taittirīya 2.6.1: 'so'kāmayata... sa tapo'tapyata' — 'He desired... He performed tapas.' (2) Aitareya 1.1.1: Ātman 'saw' (aikṣata) and created — the 'seeing' IS the tapas. (3) Ṛg Veda 10.129 (Nāsadīya Sūkta): 'In the beginning, desire arose — that was the first seed of mind' — kāma (desire) is another form of tapas. Cīyate: the verb √ci means 'to pile up, to build, to accumulate.' It evokes the image of building a fire-altar (agnicayana) — piling bricks layer by layer. Creation is Brahman 'building itself up' into the cosmic altar of the universe. The human parallel: when a yogi performs tapas, he is replicating the cosmic process in miniature — using concentrated heat/energy to transform consciousness, just as Brahman used tapas to transform itself into the universe.

This mantra outlines a compact creation-sequence: Brahman → (tapas) → anna → prāṇa → manas → satya → lokāḥ → amṛtam in karma: (1) Tapas: the creative heat/intensity — Brahman's first 'act.' (2) Anna (food/matter): the primordial substance — the material basis of creation. The Taittirīya (2.2.1) calls anna 'Brahman' itself: 'annaṁ brahmeti vyajānāt' — 'he knew food as Brahman.' (3) Prāṇa (life-force): from matter, life emerges — the vital breath that animates inert matter. (4) Manas (mind): from life, mind emerges — the capacity for thought, perception, and coordination. (5) Satya (truth / real elements): the five mahābhūtas (great elements) — the 'true' building-blocks of the physical world: space, air, fire, water, earth. (6) Lokāḥ (worlds): from the elements, the cosmic realms are constructed — earth, mid-region, heaven, and beyond. (7) Amṛtam in karma: within the worlds, beings perform actions (karma). And within those actions — if performed rightly — is a seed of immortality (amṛta). This last item is significant: it connects the aparā domain (action, ritual) to the parā domain (immortality). Even within the 'lower' knowledge, there is a hidden pointer to the 'higher.' The Upanishad is saying: don't despise the world of action — it too contains a path to the deathless.

sk: यः सर्वज्ञः सर्वविद्यस्य ज्ञानमयं तपः तस्मादेतद्ब्रह्म नामरूपमन्नं च जायते ||
ro: yaḥ · sarvajñaḥ · sarvaviḥ · yasya · jñāna-mayaṁ · tapaḥ · tasmāt · etat · brahma · nāma-rūpam · annaṁ · ca · jāyate ||
hi: जो सर्वज्ञ (omniscient) है, सर्ववित् (all-knowing — सब कुछ विशेष रूप से जानने वाला) है, जिसका तप ज्ञानमय (made of knowledge) है — उससे (तस्मात्) यह ब्रह्म (= हिरण्यगर्भ), नाम-रूप (name and form), और अन्न (food / matter) — जन्म लेते हैं।
en: He who is omniscient (sarvajña), all-knowing (sarvavid), whose tapas is made of knowledge (jñāna-maya) — from Him are born this Brahma (Hiraṇyagarbha), name-and-form (nāma-rūpa), and food (anna).

ws.e: omniscient — sarva (all) + jña (knowing); He knows everything in general — the totality of existence

ws.h: सर्ववित् / सब कुछ विशेष रूप से जानने वाला
ws.e: all-knowing in detail — sarva (all) + vid (knowing); He knows every particular — every individual being, every specific fact; Shankara distinguishes sarvajña (general omniscience) from sarvavid (particular omniscience)

ws.h: ज्ञान-स्वरूप तप / ज्ञान से बना हुआ तप
ws.e: tapas made of knowledge — His creative heat is not blind energy but conscious, knowing energy; creation is an intelligent act, not a mechanical process
name and form — the principle of individuation; what differentiates one entity from another; the entire manifest world as a display of names and forms
Brahmā / Hiraṇyagarbha — the created deity; the first being to emerge from the Imperishable; here 'brahma' (neuter/masculine) refers to the cosmic creator, not the Absolute

gr: Closing mantra of Khanda 1: this verse summarises the entire section by identifying the source of creation as the omniscient, all-knowing Being whose tapas is jñāna-maya (made of knowledge). sarvajña and sarvavid: Shankara distinguishes these: sarvajña = knows everything in general (sāmānya-jñāna); sarvavid = knows everything in particular (viśeṣa-jñāna). Together, they establish complete omniscience — Brahman knows both the forest and every tree in the forest. jñāna-mayaṁ tapaḥ — 'tapas made of knowledge': this is crucial. Brahman's creative heat is not blind force but conscious intelligence. Creation is not an accident or a mechanical process but an intelligent act. This is the Upanishadic answer to the question: why is the universe orderly? Because its source is omniscient. tasmāt etat brahma nāma-rūpam annaṁ ca jāyate — 'from Him are born Brahmā, name-and-form, and food': three products of creation — (1) Brahmā/Hiraṇyagarbha (the cosmic soul), (2) nāma-rūpa (the principle of differentiation), and (3) anna (the material substance). Together, they constitute the entire manifest universe.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_1.1.9 — This closing mantra ties together the themes of Khanda 1: the omniscient source (sarvajña sarvavid), the intelligent tapas (jñāna-maya tapas), and the triple product of creation (Brahmā + nāma-rūpa + anna). The distinction between sarvajña and sarvavid is philosophically significant — Shankara uses it to argue that Brahman has both general and particular knowledge, refuting the Sāṅkhya view that the first cause is unconscious (acetana). The phrase 'jñāna-mayaṁ tapaḥ' is unique to the Muṇḍaka and emphasises that creation is a knowing act, not a blind process. The term 'nāma-rūpa' (name and form) is the Upanishadic equivalent of the principium individuationis — the principle that differentiates one entity from another in the manifest world.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'सर्वज्ञ सर्ववित्' — ब्रह्म सामान्य (general) और विशेष (particular) दोनों ज्ञान रखता है — यह सिद्ध करता है कि जगत्-कारण चेतन (conscious) है, जड़ (inert) नहीं। 'ज्ञानमयं तपः' — ब्रह्म की सृजन-शक्ति ज्ञान-शक्ति (knowledge-power) है — अज्ञान (ignorance) नहीं।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'sarvajña sarvavid' — Brahman has both general and particular knowledge — proving the cause of the world is conscious, not inert. 'Jñāna-mayaṁ tapaḥ' — Brahman's creative power is knowledge-power, not ignorance.
advaita.ins: The universe was not created by accident or by blind force. It was created by an intelligence that knows everything — every galaxy and every atom, every species and every individual. That intelligence is still creating. It's creating you, right now.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'सर्वज्ञ सर्ववित्' — भगवान् सम्पूर्ण (complete) ज्ञानी हैं — सामान्य (general) और विशेष (particular) — कोई भी वस्तु भगवान् के ज्ञान से बाहर नहीं। 'ब्रह्म नामरूपम् अन्नं च जायते' — भगवान् से ब्रह्मा (first soul), नामरूप (individuation), और अन्न (matter) — तीनों उत्पन्न होते हैं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'sarvajña sarvavid' — the Lord has complete knowledge — general and particular — nothing is outside His knowledge. 'Brahma nāma-rūpam annaṁ ca jāyate' — from the Lord are born Brahmā (first soul), nāma-rūpa (individuation), and anna (matter).
vishisht.ins: God knows the universe the way an author knows a novel — every character, every plot-line, every word. Because He wrote it. 'Jñāna-maya tapas' — His creative energy is made of knowing. He didn't stumble into creation. He thought it into being.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'ज्ञानमयं तपः' — सृष्टि अन्ध ऊर्जा (blind energy) नहीं बल्कि ज्ञान-ऊर्जा (knowledge-energy / conscious-force) है। 'नामरूपम्' — चेतना का आत्म-विभेदन (self-differentiation) — जिससे अनेकता (multiplicity) प्रकट होती है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'jñāna-mayaṁ tapaḥ' — creation is not blind energy but knowledge-energy (conscious-force). 'Nāma-rūpam' — consciousness's self-differentiation — from which multiplicity emerges.
aurobindo.ins: The Big Bang wasn't blind. The creative force that built the universe is made of knowing — jñāna-maya tapas. Consciousness didn't accidentally produce a universe. It intelligently expressed itself AS the universe. Name-and-form is how the One became the many — and it knew exactly what it was doing.

dp.q: 🔍 Sarvajña and Sarvavid — two kinds of omniscience
dp.a: The mantra uses two words for omniscience — sarvajña and sarvavid — which Shankara distinguishes carefully: Sarvajña (सर्वज्ञ): sarva (all) + jña (knowing) = 'all-knowing' in the general sense. Brahman knows the totality — the overall nature of reality, the universal principles, the cosmic structure. This is like knowing 'the forest.' Sarvavid (सर्ववित्): sarva (all) + vid (knowing) = 'all-knowing' in the particular sense. Brahman knows every detail — every individual being, every specific event, every particular fact. This is like knowing 'every tree in the forest.' Why both are needed: an omniscient being must have both kinds of knowledge. Knowing only the general without the particular would mean not knowing any specific thing (like knowing 'humanity' without knowing any particular human). Knowing only the particular without the general would mean not seeing the pattern (like knowing every tree without seeing the forest). Brahman has both — complete knowledge at every scale. The anti-Sāṅkhya argument: Shankara uses this double omniscience to refute the Sāṅkhya school, which posits an unconscious (acetana) prakṛti as the cause of the universe. An unconscious cause cannot be sarvajña or sarvavid. The Muṇḍaka's explicit attribution of omniscience to the first cause proves the cause is conscious — Brahman, not prakṛti.

The first nine mantras of the Muṇḍaka establish the framework for the entire Upanishad: Mantras 1-2 — The lineage: Brahmā → Atharvā → Aṅgir → Satyavāha Bhāradvāja → Aṅgiras. Five links establishing the authority and antiquity of the teaching. Mantra 3 — The great question: Śaunaka asks Aṅgiras: 'What is that, knowing which, all this becomes known?' The foundational question of Vedānta. Mantras 4-5 — The two kinds of knowledge: aparā vidyā (lower) = four Vedas + six Vedāṅgas; parā vidyā (higher) = that by which the akṣara (Imperishable) is known. The Muṇḍaka's signature distinction. Mantra 6 — The akṣara described: via-negativa — invisible, ungraspable, without lineage or colour, without eyes or ears, without hands or feet; yet eternal, all-pervading, omnipresent, subtle, imperishable — the source of all beings, seen by the wise. Mantra 7 — Three similes for creation: spider-web (creation + re-absorption), earth-herbs (spontaneous emanation), person-hair (creation without diminution). Mantra 8 — The creation-sequence: Brahman → tapas → anna → prāṇa → manas → satya → lokāḥ → amṛta in karma. Mantra 9 — The omniscient source: the sarvajña-sarvavid whose jñāna-maya tapas produces Brahmā, nāma-rūpa, and anna. The arc: from authority (lineage) → to question ('knowing which, all is known?') → to answer (two knowledges; the akṣara) → to cosmogony (how the akṣara creates). Khanda 2 will turn to the practical question: what happens when people pursue aparā vidyā alone?
